speechtext: That this House condemns the intolerance and prejudice in Canadian society that damages the fabric of the nation and urges the government and all members of Parliament to play a role in strengthening understanding and respect among Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am sorry to interrupt, but I would like to tell the House that the Liberal Party will be using 10-minutes speeches followed by 5 minutes of questions and comments for all our speakers starting with the hon. member for York Centre, the justice critic. In that way we will be allowed to have more members speak on this very important subject. It is very interesting to our members, and they would all like to speak on it.

Madam Speaker, we have not yet had an opportunity to discuss this within our caucus today, but I will make a commitment that should we decide to follow suit we will indicate at the commencement of the appropriate speaker that in fact we would wish to split it between two. That certainly would not happen until after the first round of speakers.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I very much appreciate the clarity from both opposition parties. The clarity that I can give at this point is that our minister will take the full 20 minutes with a question period. Subsequently our speakers will divide as the Official Opposition is dividing: 10 and 10 with a 5-minute question period.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I wish to thank the representatives of all three parties. I realize that as far as the Liberal Party is concerned, everyone will be using only 10 minutes.
It will still be helpful to the Chair if, after the hon. member for York Centre speaks, members would remind the Chair. It would make things a lot easier.

Madam Speaker, I have moved this resolution on behalf of the Liberals because in a word not enough is being done across this land to fight bigotry, intolerance, discrimination, and racism.
Canadians possess one of the world's most fortunate and favoured countries. We have national and personal security, peaceful lives, great prosperity by any standard, spiritual freedom, democracy, personal privacy, an abundance of individual choices about how we live. Our public policies express the decency and tolerance which is a large part of our heritage.
Unlike the nations which embody the values of a single culture and empower that culture with little need to give thought or care to minoritarian interests, Canada began with an accommodation of a minority. Otherwise we would not have had this country. The fundamental principles on which Canada is built reflect the need for justice and fairness for minorities and for the individual. Over 120 years history has made us a nation of minorities. Today, no one culture or historic national group can claim the allegiance of more than half the country.
Our successful life together has given us the background, the tested and improved tools of the experience of our national life and in the human experience of our citizens, on our statute books federal and provincial, in the rules of our public institutions, to be a truly just society.
The genius of Canada is that not only did we learn to cope with our diversity, but we made it an enriching feature of our national life and not a drain on it.
It would be a betrayal of the truth, however, to set out the record of Canada as a fair and justice democracy, as I have done, without acknowledging the history of shortcomings and living up to the ideals which we call Canada; to say what I have about the openness and tolerance,

February 2, 1990
Supply
which is the greatness of Canada, without acknowledging the denial of rights, the suppression of fundamental freedoms to whole groups, and the official injustices based often sanctimoniously on sex, race, creed, region, religion, or historic origin.
The resolution before the House is not about history, because we cannot change our history and because through all of our history our eventual resolution and the national purpose was to recognize our faults, not to seek to justify them; to be more sensitive; to learn from our mistakes to the minorities in our country; and to design measures to promote fairness. Even if solutions were found too late to help the actual individuals who were victims of injustice, solutions have come and we have recognized our shortcomings and moved to improve the system.
While I do not want to dwell on the failings and shortcomings of the past, I do want to dwell on the failings and shortcomings of the present, because I am alarmed by them and because I think the whole country should be alarmed by them.
There are developments all over Canada which show the extent to which we continue to fail ourselves and our fellow Canadians. There are vast shortcomings which doom whole groups and communities to lesser status and which make a cruel joke out of the idea that everyone has an equal opportunity, or anything like an equal opportunity.

Madam Speaker, during the course of the day, my colleagues will speak of our country's shortcomings with respect to the status of women, to racial minorities and to our Native peoples.
Indeed, Madam Speaker, we intend to spend a whole day dealing with injustice towards Natives, and outlining our ideas for improving the situation to Canadians and to the government.

On the subject of native justice and the situation of the native people, I have to address and mention as a particular case the Donald Marshall inquiry, the results of which were made public over the last two weeks. That inquiry reveals the extent to which racism underlies the whole of the criminal justice system of the province of Nova Scotia. We all know that similar findings could be
made in other parts of our country. An Indian man was sentenced to prison for 11 years, totally based, according to the report, on elements of racial prejudice.
There are vast systemic injustices in our country which doom too many to less opportunity, less education, less income, less health and to shorter lives. This denial is in itself unfair, but Canada cannot afford it either. We cannot afford the loss that is caused by denying opportunity to all Canadians. We need the contribution that every individual can make when his worth is recognized and when he is given an equal opportunity.
I want to talk about large injustices and the deprivation of rights that result from them, but I also want to talk about small matters and incidents. I want to give some examples which do not in themselves take away anyone's rights or reduce anyone's individual entitlement but which affect their dignity and which diminish their pride in Canada and, in diminishing their pride in Canada, weaken the country. I want to talk about two such incidents.
One is the decision of the municipality of Sault Ste. Marie to follow the example of a few other Ontario municipalities and to go "unilingual English". Every informed citizen in that community knew that no one was asking Sault Ste. Marie to go bilingual, whatever that would have meant. The achievement of Bill 8 by the Province of Ontario does not impose requirements on any municipalities. In fact for Sault Ste. Marie it would not alter the life or the opportunities of any of the people of Sault Ste. Marie so far as provincial services are concerned.
The resolution of that community is nothing but a mean-minded statement designed, I would assume, to send a message. What is the message? Maybe it was meant to punish all of Canada's francophones for the action of the Government of Quebec in limiting, to the extent that the Government of Quebec has, free expression by anglophones in the province of Quebec.
That sad development in Quebec was also deplorable, and I and many other Canadians condemned it. Unlike the gesture by the town of Sault Ste. Marie, it was a move in the province of Quebec which actually does limit the rights of people as defined by the Supreme Court of Canada. It was a move which confirmed a sense of despair in the anglophone community of Quebec and which no doubt will be a factor in contributing to the departure from the province of Quebec of some anglo-
February 2, 1990

phones, a province which anglophones love as much as francophones who live there do.
I spent some time yesterday listening to the hot-line programs across the province of Quebec. I can tell the people of the municipality of Sault Ste. Marie that if their message was meant to encourage an improvement, it has not done so. It has only made things worse, as predictably it would. It makes it look as if this country has forgotten the openness or accommodation which is the essential ingredient of our creation as a country and the key to our good fortune as a country.
We never had the choice in Canada of being the monolithic culture which some countries are and which for some has given meaning to their national identity. We do not have that choice today. If we try to deny our diversity and suppress our differences, we will destroy ourselves.
The second example that I wanted to refer to is also a small incident in itself, small in a sense that it takes no one's rights away, but it directly affects the dignity of Canadians. I am referring to the rash of racist buttons which are being sold and eagerly bought by some in western Canada. As I say, these buttons do not take rights away, but they do attack the dignity of those they insult. They are most hurtful in their portrayal of non-whites as inferior races who are not a cultural match for whites.
This could be ignored as nonsense if it was not so hurtful. The false portrayal of the so-called sad plight of the whites in Canadian society makes a statement very far from true about the status of whites in Canada in every category of status comparison with non-whites. It is deplorable if not illegal and, while no one suffers the loss of rights, I ask the people who wear them to consider how it makes young Sikhs, young blacks, young Indians, and young orientals who were born in Canada feel when they see these insults.
In conclusion, the resolution is moved because it is not enough to identify problems. It is not enough to put in place national institutions, as we have done, or those which we will establish today to address these problems. We need to call on all Canadians who recognize what is at stake, who see that something precious is in danger, that our heritage is in danger and that our future
Supply
together is in danger, to speak out. For the worst to triumph all that is required is for good people to remain silent.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member on his very worth-while motion. It is a motion which asks this House to condemn intolerance and urges the government to play a role in strengthening understanding and respect among Canadians.
As the member knows, yesterday was the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. It is a landmark statement with respect to tolerance and understanding. It is a report which recommended tolerance in language rights, and which said that both francophones and anglophones in this country should have the right to use their own language, to have their own schools, to have their own institutions such as radio, television and health institutions. Unfortunately, 25 years later progress has been uneven.
The hon. member mentioned in his speech the recent decision by the city council at Sault Ste. Marie, a very unfortunate and prejudicial decision directed against francophones. We deplore and condemn that action. On the other hand, we have the passage of Bill 178 in Quebec, passed against the judgment of the Supreme Court by the use of the notwithstanding clause. Therefore, we have instances of intolerance and prejudice both directed against francophones and directed against anglophones.
I would ask the member if he has some suggestions to make to the House with respect to not only the situation in Sault Ste. Marie, but also to the fact that the Government of Quebec would pass a law which I believe to be an intolerant law forbidding the use of languages other than French, even though the Supreme Court suggested that the Government of Quebec might mandate the use of French but should not ban the use of other languages. It even recognized the priority of the French language in Quebec.
What recommendations can the member make to this House, since he is the initiator of this motion, to bring about greater understanding and peace, not only in Quebec between anglophones and francophones but throughout the country, and to move ahead in the true

February 2, 1990
Supply
spirit of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism?

I would like to thank my colleague for expressing so well the problems of intolerance behind some of the setbacks taking place in the country which inspired today's resolution. I hope it will lead to a greater recognition across Canada of a fact which I offer to the hon. member as at least a large part of the solution, that is recognizing what it is that has made this country great and what it is at the bottom that has made this country possible: the accommodation of difference and respect for it.
I do not want to abstract the problem from the context of the two situations that he referred to, the situation in Sault Ste. Marie and the situation with the anglophone language of signs right which was affected and diminished by Bill 178 in the province of Quebec. I deplore what happened in the province of Quebec at the time, as I deplore what happened in the city of Sault Ste. Marie.
Surely the solution is for us all to recognize as a nation what we have to gain by mutual respect and by respecting in particular those rights which are recognized by the Supreme Court of Canada.
We do not build a nation and then sit back and enjoy it. Building a nation is something that has to be done every day. We should be alert and vigilant every day to the suppression of rights, to insults to minority groups, and we should take steps when we see them to call them what they are.

Madam Speaker, I am sharing my time with the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan).
I welcome the opportunity to take part in today's debate. As a people, Canadians commit themselves to the creation of a society that ensures equality and justice for all, regardless of race or ethnic origin.
We find these words in the preamble to the Acknowledgment text signed by the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney).
Madam Speaker, I would like to know to whom these words apply. If we look at what is happening in this country, the principles of equality and justice for all
seem at times, I would even say all too often, to be ignored by the very people whose mandate it is to uphold these principles.
Madam Speaker, I ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis), where was justice in the trial of Donald Marshall in Halifax? Where was equality for all, when Donald Marshall, son of the Grand Chief of the Micmac Indians, was arrested? And this is only one of many cases.

Two research studies done in Nova Scotia have shown that prejudice against the natives and blacks is prevalent and leads to discrimination against them in the justice system.
A study by Dr. Wilson Head, president of the Federation on Race Relations in Toronto, and Donald Clair-mont, a Dalhousie University sociologist, state clearly that "blacks have been viewed as undesirable, unable to adapt to a cold climate, shiftless, lazy, and fit only for slavery and as servants of the wealthy."

Madam Speaker, the intolerance and prejudice that exist in our society are unacceptable. It is high time the government got the situation under control, before it is too late. We must invest in citizenship programs. We must provide new immigrants, who often become the scapegoats of our frustrations, the resources they need to acquire a better understanding of the culture in which they have chosen to live. We must give them the means to adjust to their new country by helping them acquire a good knowledge of the language of daily life. Above all, however, and this may be where we have failed most, we must encourage Canadians to learn to know and accept Canada's new image.
Madam Speaker, it is important for various ethnic and racial groups to be visible in all areas that influence the image the government wishes to project of Canadian society. We need them in the government, at the decision-making level; in the media, to help prepare programs and series that are representative of the new Canadian reality; and in education, at all levels. If the government really wants to wipe out inequality and intolerance in this country, it must set an example. All Canadians must have their place in all sectors of our society.
February 2, 1990

Madam Speaker, it is unacceptable that in 1990, I should still receive letters from people who are being denied-one wonders on what authority-the right to be different.
I would like to read a short passage from a five-page letter I received from one of my constituents. I may point out that this person was employed in the Public Service. She has been in Canada for 25 years, and her only fault was that she was an immigrant. She explained in her letter that she tried to open the window of a room filled with cigarette smoke. I apologize for the unparliamentary language, but this is a daily part of some people's lives.
So I beg the indulgence of the Chair and my colleagues. I quote:
"I asked for permission to open the window (since I did not have the right to touch any window or door and I always had to ask for permission, just in my case, but if any other employees did, it was all right. -Then the cleaner jumped on me, shouting and calling me a 'damn immigrant woman. Why don't you go back to your land of camels? You have come to take our place, damn you. You won't stay here long.'" She continues: "I asked him, 'How do you know that I won't stay here?' He answered, 'I have been told and everyone knows, damn you.' I went to see the manager. He blushed and told me, 'This is a democracy. The majority wins.'"

The letter continues. This is not an isolated case. I am certain that everyone in this room knows of someone being abused in some way. We even do it in our ethnic and racial jokes. We never think of the effect it can have on the group we are joking about.
If we really want our nation to stay one, it is high time the government publicly condemned intolerance and prejudice and played a leading role in strengthening understanding and respect among Canadians and those who aspire to become Canadians.
The government must be pro-active. It must stop reacting to crisis and start weaving bonds between all, young and old, all professions and all cultures, all religions and all races. If we can do it to fight a war, why can we not do it to guarantee peace? What does this say for our society?

I am very concerned when a society has reached a point where a disenchanted employee can take the liberty to give the weather forecast, slipping in a message of intolerance like this, and I quote:

"Today, mainly sunny with racists. Then clouding over this afternoon with a chance of flurries and Nazis."

Those were the words used.
Madam Speaker, throughout Canada, intolerance is on the rise. Now we must stop saying so, playing the ostrich and hoping it will go away. We must take concrete action. We can no longer afford to wait for miracle solutions. The government must act, take a stand and provide support wherever this positive action is taken.
Madam Speaker, how can we tolerate racist buttons whose purpose is to denigrate another human being? Have we become so indifferent to what is going on around us? When will the government admit that however small the offense, even if it is just a button, it is still an offense and often it is an accumulation of small incidents that finally cause peace to break down, just as water eats away at a rock?

I do not think at this time that I need to pinpoint events where intolerance and prejudice are, sad to say, daily news. I condemn this and urge the government to play its role in strengthening understanding and respect among Canadians.

In conclusion, I would like to quote another great Canadian: "If we want to be independent and proud, we must keep this country united."

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville (Mrs. Maheu) for her excellent speech on Canadian citizenship and what it really means. I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). First, his motion:
That this House condemn the intolerance and prejudice in Canadian
society that damages the fabric of the nation and urge the government

February 2, 1990
Supply
and all members of Parliament to play a role in strengthening
understanding and respect among Canadians.
As a Canadian citizen who is a fourth-generation Franco-Ontarian, I have often lived with prejudice and I am very sorry to see how much prejudice some people in Quebec have against their English-speaking fellow citizens. This week I was greatly distressed by the negative reaction exemplified in Sault Ste. Marie. As a former alderman, I know that small groups often lobby municipal councils for one cause or another; 99.9 per cent of the time, these causes are very worthwhile and municipal councils often present motions to accommodate groups and thus show their attitude to some event or other. In the case of Sault Ste. Marie, they had nothing to gain; it was negative, very negative. There was no reason for it to happen. I am afraid that the next resolution in a place like Sault Ste. Marie will be about people's colour. Then will it be religion? Canada was built by French, British, European, Asian and other immigrants. Because of intolerance, we came here to America to find a better world. And it is really deplorable that a generation or two or three later, the descendants of immigrants present such negative resolutions. So I congratulate the two hon. members who spoke before me for their presentation on tolerance in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in response to the hon. member's motion I wish to reaffirm this Canadian government's commitment to the principles of tolerance, respect and understanding for all Canadians.
About three decades ago Martin Luther King, Jr., said: "Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere." This is why we have been working with groups across the country to eliminate intolerance, racism and racial discrimination in order to build a more just and caring society. It goes without saying that the first salvo in the battle against intolerance and racial discrimination is the acknowledgement of the presence of these evils in our society. We know there is prejudice in our society. We
have all come into contact with it. But government alone cannot eliminate intolerance and racism.
We must have the co-operation of like-minded citizens. A recent incident shows that we have many Canadians willing to speak out against prejudice. Hon. members are aware of the racist pin being sold in Calgary. Its sale was another example of the intolerance we must overcome. The sale of this pin also brought home the fact that Canadians will not tolerate such an attitude. The swift reaction to this pin was most encouraging. The community came together and spoke out against its blatant prejudice. Editorial writers, columnists, the mayor of Calgary, the Alberta Human Rights Commission, the business community, all have spoken out against the blatant prejudice of these products. I myself issued a very strong condemnation of this very abominable behaviour.
The reaction to an incident such as this demonstrates the true heart of Canada. Canadians not only in Calgary, not only in Alberta, but throughout the country made their voices heard. They spelled it out. Racist symbols and the hatred they generate will not be tolerated.
We know the majority of Canadians celebrate the rich cultural diversity of Canada, but this government wants to ensure that cultural diversity, which we have declared in law to be a fundamental characteristic of Canada, is realized in fact.

Madam Speaker, Canada is lucky to be a young and free country, founded on the principles of openness and tolerance. We are a peace-loving people, a society that has always put the well-being and interests of its citizens above any other considerations, a country that has always cultivated the values of equality.
Entire generations of Canadians of all origins chose Canada because they knew they could live in peace and prosper in this country. They did far more than that, however. They helped make this country what it is today. It is largely thanks to them that today, Canada is a prosperous nation and one of the world's great industrial powers. It is also thanks to them that today, the Canadian character stands for something unique in this world, based on generosity, solidarity, and respect for others.
February 2, 1990



The multiculturalism policy of this government has created a vision of this country. It is a vision of nationbuilding and of national unity. We are building political and national unity out of our cultural diversity. Our diversity is what strengthens us. This is nation-building; this is equality; this is social justice. For this government multiculturalism is not simply the recognition of cultural diversity. For us it is an egalitarian and anti-racist philosophy and program.
Philosophically multiculturalism is a way of thinking about cultural diversity which emphasizes that all citizens have equal political, social and cultural rights. It views cultural differences as features of social life which must be incorporated into all aspects of the functioning of the state. To do otherwise would be to allow our cultural differences to destabilize society. With regard to racism, multiculturalism holds that it is at best pseudoscientific nonsense and at worst a blatant fraud.
Programmatically multiculturalism seeks to preserve, enhance and share the elements of cultural diversity by, among other things, supporting the teaching of heritage languages, establishing chairs of ethnic studies and encouraging various artistic productions. In this endeavour it recognizes the need for active participation with the community, with institutions and with all levels of government as we pursue the important task of nationbuilding. Multiculturalism is also dedicated to the eradication of racism by relentlessly exposing its pseudo-scientific and fraudulent assumptions and by bringing about changes in social institutions that perpetuate inequality on the basis of cultural and physical differences.
This government introduced the first Employment Equity Act. It also established a committee to advise the Treasury Board on the representation of visible minorities in the Public Service. We opened up the Canadian Jobs Strategy to enable more immigrant women to benefit from language and skills training. We have addressed the grievances of Japanese Canadians, brought into law the Canadian Multiculturalism Act and introduced Bill C-18 to establish the new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. This new department will strengthen national integration and national identity and will enable all Canadians to participate fully and without discrimination in building the nation's future.

It will work with community groups to break down the barriers and limitations that deny some Canadians full participation in day to day community life.
This nation has a rich cultural and ethnic diversity. It must be allowed to be given full expression in terms of our citizenship. Full citizenship demands full participation. It demands equal access for each one of us and we will not accept any less.
We have been working very vigorously to make Canadians much more aware of the benefits that this brings to the nation and to show how much more productive we have become, how much more challenging we are, how much more competitive we are when we use our full human resource.
We have been building partnerships so that multiculturalism is mainstream for every institution of the community. We have been examining how we can, through this program and with this cross-government commitment, examine every institution to see how they can be helped to become more familiar with it, allow more participation and derive more benefit from having this full and open participation. And, we have been making significant progress.
Our Canadian Multiculturalism Act provides a strong legislative base to promote social justice and equal opportunity for all Canadians. There is an increasing appreciation that the task of nation building is profoundly influenced by our social and cultural relations. Recognizing this, our Multiculturalism Act pledges that the Canadian government go beyond establishing equality rights. It promotes a multicultural and open society where all Canadians can participate and can contribute to their fullest extent.
The act strengthens our Canadian identity. It contributes to our understanding and acceptance of each other's uniqueness. It commits the Canadian government to ensuring that all Canadians can participate fully and without discrimination in defining and building Canada's future. Our multiculturalism policy will help Canada enter the 21st century with emphasis on the positive aspects of coexistence among culturally diverse communities.
The act is a direct result of our efforts to develop a model society. We have developed a society where diversity is acknowledged as a strength and where

February 2, 1990
Supply
freedom and tolerance, fairness and courtesy, compassion and common sense are overriding characteristics. This is what we mean by cultural integration, not the form of assimilation which has been tried in other parts of the world. We believe in the preservation and the enrichment of our society for all Canadians. This has become a unique world model being examined and followed by nations around the globe.
The act that we brought forward states that multicul-turalism is a fundamental characteristic of our society. That is a key statement of government policy, because it establishes for the first time in law that cultural diversity must be taken into consideration in the decision making of all government institutions.
Our new Governor General, His Excellency, the Right Hon. Ramon Hnatyshyn, expressed the identity of our country in his inaugural address this past Monday:
The ability to change and move with history has been bred into the Canadian character. We are an Atlantic country, a Pacific Rim country, and we are linked almost mystically with the north. Rather than locking ourselves into rigid definitions and ways of acting, we have moulded ourselves into a complex and subtle nation.

The Department for which I am responsible has always worked very hard, especially in recent years, to fight discrimination and promote equal opportunities for all citizens.
For instance, in recent years the Women's Program at the Department of the Secretary of State has provided financial and many other types of support for many organizations involved in promoting women's rights. We have placed special emphasis on promoting economic equality, access to social justice and services, and the full and complete participation of women in society.
For a number of years the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and federal and provincial human rights legislation have helped to reduce various forms of discrimination and inequality affecting women. Of course, much remains to be done, but in this respect Canada compares well with most other countries.
Earlier I spoke of a racist incident that brought a strong response from many Canadians. Now I wish to say a few words about the government's formal efforts to combat racist attitudes.
We have a race relations and cross-cultural understanding program. It supports efforts by Canadian institutions, community groups and individuals to eliminate discrimination and foster understanding. The program encourages institutions in fields such as justice, education, labour, social services and the media to better serve our multicultural society. It helps community organizations promote equality and mutual understanding. It provides financial assistance for research and development of cross-culture training methods.
Under this program, in partnership with the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, we have carried out several initiatives designed to help police forces become more sensitive to our country's cultural diversity. We have assisted the Federation of Canadian Municipalities in implementing its own municipal race relations program. We have supported such activities as the establishment of the National Action Committee on Race Relations. The program has also assisted the Canadian Human Rights Foundation in helping promote awareness in the legal community of the legal basis of multiculturalism.
Under the program, we held a national symposium on the impact of media on race relations. Hon. members will recall that only two days ago I tabled a bill in the House to establish the Canadian Race Relations Foundation with its principal office in metropolitan Toronto.
Hon. members will also be familiar with the government's initiatives marking the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination on March 21. We will continue to use special days like March 21 to focus attention on the issues.
The Prime Minister of Canada, speaking at the installation of our new Governor General on Monday, said:
Canada has constitutional promises to keep, multiple cultures to
reconcile and regional disparities to redress. The task of nation-
February 2, 1990

building is often difficult, and its fruits are rarely perfect. But they
are the culmination of generous contributions to a noble cause-the
building of a strengthened and progressive nation.
I share with the Prime Minister a vision of a new Canada, a Canada where our different customs and traditions, our origins and colour of our skin are a wonderful and varied expression of our common humanity. We are striving for a diversity to which we all contribute, a diversity from which we all benefit.

To achieve harmony among our various cultural groups remains one of the fundamental objectives of Canadian society.
Madam Speaker, I am very proud to have been given a chance to work towards this goal. Considerable progress has been made this year.

I have noticed a lot of good will, a lot of realism, a lot of understanding. We will soon be bringing forward a Canadian multiculturalism advisory committee. It will bring forward individuals representative of the varied institutions that we will be working with: labour, business, the voluntary sector, education, private and public sectors, health and social services. It will be an opportunity for us to examine institutions within the community to see how they can, once and for all, allow the full participation of all of our citizens.
It is an area of our endeavour of which we are particularly proud. There are still far too many incidents that are disquietening, with distressing undercurrents. We are developing initiatives to address concerns such as those raised by the Marshall inquiry in a very proactive manner. We have been consulting actively. For example, I have been to Halifax four times in the last year.
We have some very exciting ideas. I signed an agreement this past year with the city of Halifax on a very important initiative. We are looking to bring forward more important programs to help create equality in this society.
Wherever we turn, I have been forceful and vigilant on behalf of the government. I am pleased to say that Canadians from coast to coast have been very helpful in wanting to get more involved in the issue. I am thankful
Supply
that we have an opportunity today, not only to reach all members of Parliament, but to be able sensitize the entire Canadian community to the benefits of what we are talking about. To keep a situation of second-class citizenship in the country is dangerous. It promotes racial tensions, and it is something we must avoid at all costs.

Madam Speaker, an initiative that was supposed to deal with intolerance and prejudice in the workplace was the government's Employment Equity Act passed in 1986. This law was supposed to implement affirmative action programs for women, visible minorities, aboriginal people and disabled people. Two years after the passage of the act very little progress has been made, and that was pointed out in the annual report pursuant to the act which was tabled in this House at the end of 1989.
Following the tabling of that report, Max Yalden, Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, stated that very little progress had been made. That criticism was seconded by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and the Canadian Ethnocultural Council.
In his speech the minister made some very strong statements against prejudice, and I congratulate him on that. There were some very good statements.
If he is sincere in what he says, will he not recommend to his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration who is responsible for the Employment Equity Act, to amend that act so it can be an effective act? The stated purposes in the act are very good, but the act is inadequate in that it does not have effective sanctions or an effective enforcement agency.
If the minister is sincere and if the government is sincere in trying to do the things that they say they stand for, surely they will want to amend that act so that we will not continue to get the kind of reports that we got this year. For example, even companies like the Canada Post Corporation and the CBC, all Crown companies, were getting failing grades against all target groups such as women, visible minorities, aboriginal people and disabled people. They had a horrible record, according to this report. It included private companies as well.
Would he not support an initiative to amend that law to make it do what he really wants to do?

February 2, 1990

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace will know that I served as the parliamentary secretary at the time the employment equity bill was brought forward.
I have heard the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration respond that they are currently examining the whole process of what has been implemented and the effect of it on the program. In a very short period of time, she will be coming to her cabinet colleagues and discussing with them an opportunity of perhaps further strengthening the process.
I am certainly awaiting what she will bring forward from within her area of responsibility. I will indicate that those who have heard me across the country, wherever I have been, certainly have not found me to be lacking in the understanding I have of the inequality I have found.
I am not new to this issue. I have worked as a volunteer in the field all my life. If there is one thing that I carry with me from my youth it is a remembrance of the intolerance, the lack of understanding and the lack of opportunity that I faced as a member of a cultural community at that time. Many members of my community have now overcome it, but it is still blatant and present for many others.
What I have said as an individual and offering the leadership of the federal government is that we have been prepared to examine every institution beginning with ourselves and demand that once and for all it provide full equality, full access, and full understanding. That is what our citizenship demands and we will accept no less.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There will be five minutes left in the questions and comment period following the minister's speech after Question Period.

It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30(5), the House will now proceed to statements by Members, pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Madam Speaker, for many months now my office has been offering a sympathetic ear to small business in my riding. Their concerns are not simply the monetary expenses which they will be confronted with in administering the GST. They are also concerned about the logistics and added pressures of dealing with the ever-deeper reach which this government is making into their lives and livelihood.
For example, tax preparers will be forced to submit pages 5 and 6 of every individual return for 1989 on green paper. Normally blue paper is accepted for income tax returns but pages 5 and 6 are the GST refund application forms. The government seems unable and unwilling to take its time to sort these pages out on its own. Instead they are placing the monumental task of submitting 2.5 million prepared forms on the backs of the tax preparers.
I suggest to the government that the Minister of Finance has set these tasks and expenses upon the backs of the small businessmen of Canada at his and his government's peril, and a further frustration for small business.

Madam Speaker, today I would like to draw the attention of the House to the outstanding performance of Quebec athletes at the Commonwealth Games in Auckland. I would like to pay tribute to Guillaume Leblanc of Rimouski, who yesterday won a gold medal in the 30-kilometre racewalk. He finished the race in two hours, eight minutes and 28 seconds. This was Guillaume Leblanc's third time at the Olympics, after Seoul and Los Angeles.
I would also like to mention the excellent work done by Joanne Falardeau of Quebec City and Denyse Julien of Rouyn-Noranda, who won a bronze medal in badminton doubles. These achievements are the result of

incredible perseverance and hard work, something only exceptionally dynamic athletes can manage. I am sure that hon. members will wish to join me today in applauding these athletes from Quebec who honour our country with their success.

Madam Speaker, radio and TV today announced that Prime Minister de Klerk of South Africa will he says soon release Nelson Mandela and legalize the African National Congress and other organizations which have been banned. This is something that people all over the world have worked for.
But we should be especially thankful to the courageous and mainly peaceful struggle of the South African people, blacks and whites, Christians and communists, who have struggled for half a century for justice against apartheid. We should thank also the United Nations which made apartheid illegal under international law and encouraged sanctions by many countries to put pressure on the apartheid government.
We should also look to the future because the African National Congress Charter, which was banned as a subversive document, calls among other things for universal literacy in a government drive against illiteracy, for health care, for housing and these are all matters in which we could copy the Charter of the African National Congress.

Madam Speaker, yesterday the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship, the hon. Gerry Weiner tabled a bill to establish a Canadian Race Relations Foundation. Tabling this legislation reinforces the government's commitment to equality for all Canadians as expressed in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in the Multiculturalism Act.
The foundation will serve as a national resource for community groups, governments, institutions, the private sector, researchers and the general public to further. their understanding of racism and racial disrimination in Canadian society. The foundation, whose principal office will be located in the Toronto area, will be instrumental in the elimination of racism and all forms of racial discrimination in Canadian society.
I urge the hon. members to support the new foundation in its effort to combat racism wherever it exists.

Madam Speaker, the role of the CBC in Canada is no less vital today than it has been at any time in our history. Canadians who value this great national institution should, may I say with great respect, wake up to the fact that the CBC as we have known it in this country is now about to be destroyed. May I suggest, Madam Speaker, by a deliberate design of the government opposite, primarily by the Minister of Finance who, in his headlong rush to meet his economic priorities, is destroying a part of Canada's heritage, destroying that institution that has provided the nation with a mirror of itself and mirrors this nation to the rest of the world, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
On Tuesday, the CBC announced cuts of $140 million over four years laying off 500 employees. On Wednesday, the Minister of Communications suggested CBC should get out of the advertising business, a loss of $360 million a year, and today we find out that childrens' programming is being cut by the CBC. There is pitifully little enough good children's programming available to our children in this nation. There is fewer still of good Canadian programming. Let's stop the destruction of Canada's culture and a great national Canadian institution.

Madam Speaker, government and landowners should seek every opportunity to plant more trees. Presently there are a variety of federal and provincial government programs to assist reforestation. While these programs have proven quite successful, we still face a tremendous opportunity and challenge for replenishing and expanding our forests. Canada has vast areas of rural wasteland in regions

February 2, 1990
where the climate is ideal for growing trees. This land should be planted with trees.
The National Soil Conservation Program and associated agreements with the provinces offer another opportunity to stimulate reforestation. Under these new programs highly erodable land will no longer be used for production of annual field crops. Trees could be a part of the permanent ground cover for such lands. The largest challenge and responsibility falls on individual landowners. I urge those with unproductive or erosion-prone rural lands to make a resolution for the 1990s. That resolution should be "Plant Trees".

Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak on a serious concern. We know that sometime this month the Minister of Finance is going to introduce his budget for the upcoming year. We also have been told by the same minister that he does not have the time to meet with ordinary Canadians. This year the hon. minister has chosen to prepare his budget behind closed doors surrounded only by his nearest and dearest.
The government can promise Boeing $150 million prior to the budget but it cannot meet with ordinary Canadians. Perhaps since the minister refuses to meet and consult with the rest of us, he will simply announce in this House what he will do and what workers should do with regard to negotiating higher raises to counteract the GST. You know the GST, Madam Speaker. That is the tax on which Jean Chretien will not give his position.
Oh, oh!

Should northern workers start bargaining for benefits to compensate for the impending loss of northern tax benefits? Should other workers be concerned about what is going to happen to UI premiums? What is going to happen to medicare and health programs across this country? When is the minister going to talk with ordinary Canadians and tell us what our future is all about?

Madam Speaker, the report of the Royal Commission on the Donald
Marshall case is forcing Canadians to re-assess their attitudes and examine the extent of intolerance, discrimination and prejudice in Canadian society.
Aboriginal people are still in some parts of the country confronted daily with racial prejudice. It is hard to for aboriginal people to watch television movies in which our people are slow, dumb, vicious, blood-thirsty and speak in one- syllables. It is difficult to read old books which portray aboriginal people as "primitive" and "uncivilized". The recently re-released book of Pierre Berton, The Mysterious North is a modem example of old attitudes. Originally published in 1956 its descriptions of aboriginal people are offensive.
In a preface to the 1989 edition, Berton acknowledges that attitudes have changes toward the north and aboriginal people since the 1950s. While the book may be entertaining reading for most people-it won the Governor General's award-its repackaging is painful reading for aboriginal people.

Madam Speaker, in the past couple of weeks we have had a couple of announcements coming out of Prince Edward Island. Both of these announcements were made for the best of reasons. They were made by two major corporations, McCain's and Irving's.
They were really announcements of how positive we are in Atlantic Canada. Both of these companies are expanding in Prince Edward Island for the very best of reasons, namely, that we can in Atlantic Canada do what we do best, do it better than any part of the world and compete on a very even and level playing field.
With these announcements nothing was done at the expense of the industry in any part of Canada nor will they endanger the industry in any other part of Canada. I am very proud of what the Irving and McCain corporations are doing in Prince Edward Island. I think as Canadians we can be very proud of the fact that we can compete on the international market.
February 2, 1990

Madam Speaker, the temperature in the National Capital Region dropped overnight and as the final ingredient for another successful Winterlude the weather kicked into gear.
Thanks to all the volunteers and organizers, the people of the National Capital Region and the more than the million tourists who come to the nation's capital to participate in the ten-day party, Winterlude, 1990, can begin.
This year's theme is distinctly Denmark and promises to be the best ever. So put on your toque and mitts and have some fun. See the ice sculptures, watch the races and the fireworks, go for a skate on the canal while feasting on a beaver tail. Take a sleigh ride and cheer on the participants in the many competitions. Laugh with the clowns and watch the barrel jumpers. Enjoy the culinary dishes available at every turn. More than 300 events will take place over the next ten days so participate and enjoy.
In my constituency of Nepean we too will have programs. Hot air balloons and kites will fly the air tonight. The nation's capital is ready. The people are energetic. The weather is perfect.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this morning we have every reason to rejoice, since President de Klerk of South Africa has made a start with reforms, announcing he will release leader Nelson Mandela and showing his willingness to negotiate in order to unban the Africa National Congress and other factions that want recognition of human rights in South Africa. This step is partly the result of pressure by Commonwealth countries.
Since 1985, our Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) have worked very hard to fight apartheid and to support recognition of the rights of our black brothers in South Africa. I want to congratulate them, and I also wish to mention the courage shown by our Prime Minister at the Commonwealth Conference in Vancouver in October 1987, and on so many other occasions.
I would urge President de Klerk to perseveres, and I think all Canadians should be delighted with the first step made this morning.

Madam Speaker, in this morning's Journal de Montreal, the federal Minister of Labour (Mr. Corbeil), who is the minister responsible for Montreal, said: "If Montreal's economy is in decline, it is mainly due to an ignorant labour force."
Madam Speaker, "an ignorant labour force". Is the Labour Minister speaking on behalf of the federal government when he says that about the working people of Montreal? Do his colleagues here from Quebec agree with the Minister of Labour of Canada? This morning, Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister is in Chambly for a by-election. Does the Prime Minister agree with his minister that the Montreal labour force is ignorant? If the Prime Minister agrees, will he repeat it to the voters of Chambly this morning? Or if he completely disagrees with his Labour Minister who said that this morning in Chambly, will he apologize on behalf of his minister? It is quite important, Madam Speaker!

Madam Speaker, with the announcements received today from South Africa's President de Klerk about proposed new directions toward the elimination of racial discrimination in that country, the world takes another giant step forward in the historic journal of global civilization.
This will be encouraging good news for all nations but particularly so for the Commonwealth countries whose efforts to promote reform in South Africa have been diligent and dedicated for a very long time. Canada has played a major role in these respects and credit is due both to our Prime Minister and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for their personal stands and influ-

February 2, 1990
Oral Questions
ence on these issues leading up to today's dramatic events.
Surely this profound progress on the world's stage in which Canada has had a part will intensify the commitment and the creative energy of all Canadians to the continued building of our own country as a leading model among nations of racial and linguistic tolerance in a caring, compassionate and civilized society.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question this Friday morning is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The Environment Minister, who is not here this morning, is well known as the great expert on by-elections. He promised his own riding more than $160 million to ensure his own election on June 20, 1988. But as the Deputy Prime Minister well knows, only the Prime Minister's prestige friends are entitled to such special treatment.
After promising for months that he would find a solution to the problem of the PCB containers which are still in Saint-Basile-le-Grand, the Environment Minister told the people of that community very recently that the cost would be so huge that it could not be justified, even in an election campaign. That is what the Environment Minister said.
My question for the Deputy Prime Minister is: If the government can provide a safe seat for the Environment Minister, why is it unable to provide safe living conditions for the people of Saint-Basile-le-Grand?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment I would remind the right hon. member that the federal government has already contributed some $2 million in services to the people in the area and, furthermore, it is agreed to provide compensation in partnership with the province of Quebec. Those negotiations are still occurring. I might add that we have not as yet received a package from the
province of Quebec indicating what its request will be of us.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I address the Deputy Prime Minister, hoping for a reply. To show his alleged commitment to the environment and recycling programs, the government is recycling its old promises.
In 1988, the government promised to convert part of the firing range in Chambly into a green space. Now the Environment Minister is making the same promise again for this by-election. But only two years ago, eight soldiers were injured by a buried shell which exploded when they made a campfire. Will the Environment Minister stop manipulating the voters of Chambly? Why did he not ensure that the place was completely safe before recycling his own program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. Of course, as he knows we have reached an arrangement whereby 85 hectares of the 512-hectare St. Bruno site will be transferred under the jurisdiction of the parks department. It is on the hillside to enable public access to that area which the public had been requesting for a number of years.
I would like to assure him that that range is only used for firing with blank ammunition. No live shells are used in the firing exercises at St. Bruno.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to remind the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that the incident to which he referred did not occur at the St. Bruno firing range. It occurred at Val Cartier which, of course, is quite a different place. So we can assure the public that there is no danger in the public utilization of the St. Bruno range. I am sure that it is going to be a very welcome addition for recreational activities for the people of Chambly.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to know that once more this government, when it comes to a by-election, shoots nothing but blanks in order to get votes.

Oh, Oh!
February 2, 1990
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Tbrner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to put the following question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Only he can answer a question on general government policy.
The Minister of the Environment, using a metaphor that the minister has just used, has bombed in his portfolio as Minister of the Environment. He is too busy on by-elections to concentrate on the big picture and his big program. For months we have been told that the government has a new plan for the environment. For months we have been told that the government has real spending plans for the environment. For months we have been told to wait for the Minister of Finance because he and the Minister of the Environment, when the Budget is brought down, are going to have a great new environmental protection program for Canada. Now we read, and I want the Deputy Prime Minister to comment on these reports, that the Minister of the Environment has failed and has fired blanks with his colleagues, particularly the Minister of Finance, and there will be no such program.
Would he confirm or deny those press reports? Would he assure us, hopefully, that that great plan for the environment that we have been waiting for from this newly-minted minister will finally see the light of day for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to shooting blanks, the best example of that is the performance of the Leader of the Opposition in Question Period.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Again, the Leader of the Opposition is relying upon The Globe and Mail for his research. I suppose his research staff has left him already because he is looking for a new job. The fact is that the-
Where is your answer?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will give you an answer. As a matter of fact, the Leader of the Opposition had two
Oral Questions
good answers to two very legitimate questions. I want to compliment both members for enlightening the minister.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If you will just give a little time, I will answer the question.
How much time?
Stop rushing him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If you would like to sit down and get up later on-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am momentarily speechless. Perhaps the minister could finish his answer.
He hasn't started yet.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition should stop relying on The Globe and Mail for his questions in Question Period.
I can assure the hon. Leader of the Opposition, his colleagues, and the people of the country that the Minister of the Environment is working on a new environmental policy which will be all-encompassing. It is a very major priority. It was outlined in the Speech from the Throne and, as in so many other cases, when this government makes a commitment, it delivers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Labour who is responsible for Montreal.
Three years after the publication of the Picard report suggesting a development plan for Montreal, noted the renowned economist Laurent Picard who wrote this report advises us now that it is being implemented in Toronto and not in Montreal.
Could the govemement advise us whether it needs to take a geography course to find out where Montreal is really located? Could the Minister explain to me what stopped the government from implementing the recommendations of this report?

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make it clear to the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville that contrary to

Oral Questions
the previous administration, this government has dealt effectively with the situation which has developed on the Island of Montreal over the past few years.
As a first step, the government passed a legislation dealing with pharmaceuticals which the opposition had fought tooth and nail and which now represents nearly $700 million in investments on the Island of Montreal.
Something the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Car-tierville might be unaware of, this government has contributed to the prosperity of the riding she lives and works in by granting $43 million to Canadair to help this corporation get involve in the production of the stretched Jet liner and create 2,000 new jobs in that industry.
The government I represent has located in the Montreal area the Space Agency which should be worth $3 billion to the Montreal economy over the next few years and which, as recently as last Friday, awarded a contract to the Spar Aerospace corporation in Montreal, resulting in some $140 million investments in that area.
When one considers the situation now with what it was previously, Mr. Speaker, one realizes that the level of unemployment is much lower on the Montreal Island.
Shirley Maheu (Saint-Laurent-Cartierville): Mr. Speaker, I wish I had as much time as the minister!
By the way, most drug manufacturers are based in Toronto.
I should like to know why Mr. Picard, the author of the report, has seen fit to focus on the inaction of the very government that commissioned his report. Just what does the government plan to do in the immediate future to implement the Picard report recommendations?

Mr. Speaker, our government will continue to do the excellent job it has been doing in recent years. Again I would remind the seemingly forgetful Member for Saint-Laurent that our government made a major contribution towards the establishment of an agency called CITEC in her riding.
With respect to Montreal East, Mr. Speaker, which happens to be the island's worse off sector as a result of years of neglect on the part of our colleagues opposite,
last year we invested $13 million in the Industrial Recovery Program for East End Montreal which attracted private sector investments of $65 million.
Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat in the House that, contrary to Mr. Picard's statement, a man whose professional credentials I duly acknowledge, the federal government is not primarily responsible for the economic recovery of the Island of Montreal. The impetus should originate from local circles and we intervene only to grease the wheels, not to set them in motion.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Before the election in October, 1988, the Prime Minister made several very strong statements. He said on October 15, "We are prepared to subject every federal undertaking and every undertaking on federal lands to a full environmental impact study". On October 20, he said: "No area is higher on our environmental priority list than the Great Lakes themselves". On October 1, he said: "We stand for a cleaner, safer environment".
In the Throne Speech, this government's last Throne Speech, we were told, and I quote: "The world itself is facing an environmental challenge of unprecedented magnitude". These are serious words but there is no serious action. This government is doing nothing. It now appears that even the Minister of the Environment does not have the support of his colleagues. I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, when will he give this House a firm deadline for the introduction of the government's environmental plan?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I think all members of the House know, it is exceedingly important that this country have the kind of legislation in place which will ensure that decisions of government respecting the environment made in the future will have clarity and certainty with respect to the responsibilities of this
February 2, 1990

government, the responsibilities of the provinces and all the interested parties.
As we know, the ERP guidelines which we inherited when we came to power in 1984 have clearly been found to be inadequate. As a result of that, the Minister of the Environment has committed himself to the formulation of new legislation which is part of an environmental agenda. That legislation and the environmental agenda require the co-operation and participation of all departments within this government. It is absolutely essential that this legislation and this agenda be drafted in such a way that we avoid the mistakes and messes created in the past by that party over there. Therefore, we are ensuring that the legislation be done in such a fashion. Although it may be later than we would wish, it will meet the test when it is there.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Deputy Prime Minister.
All that we can hear and all that Canadians can hear from the answer to the previous question is that this government was inadequate in 1984 in dealing with the environment, inadequate in 1988 and inadequate again in 1990. They cannot get their act together.
Six years later, nothing.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are fed up waiting for the government to act.
Let me ask the Deputy Prime Minister something more specific. Earlier this week the city of Toronto committed itself to a 20 per cent reduction in carbon emissions by the year 2005. This was something the minister of energy rejected despite the recommendations of many experts.
Will this government take some real action and commit itself to a reduction of carbon emissions by the year 2005?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member refers to the government's record on the environment as being inadequate, she is really misstating the facts. Quite frankly,
Oral Questions
since this government came into power we have brought in a Canadian Environmental Protection Act that stands as a model in the world, a made in Canada acid rain control program. We have the toughest controls on car emissions of any country in the world.
When it comes to water, we released a comprehensive federal water strategy, a $110 million clean-up of the St. Lawrence River, a $75 million clean-up of the Halifax Harbour, a clean-up of the Sydney tar ponds. We have negotiated and signed the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement with the United States, created six new national parks, $106 million to South Moresby, the Rouge River Wilderness Park and created the first national marine park at Bruce Peninsula.
In addition to that, the leadership internationally has been outstanding both by the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Environment.

I have a supplementary for the Deputy Prime Minister. Canadians are fed up with the empty promises of this government. Throughout the electoral campaign the government kept saying it would launch effective environmental assessment programs. Last fall the minister promised to introduce this kind of legislation. When will the minister table his bill?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I enunciated on behalf of the Minister of the Environment were not promises; they were undertakings and they were accomplishments.
As has been pointed out in the Speech from the Throne and has been enunciated by the Minister of the Environment, he is working on a comprehensive plan. Included in that will be legislation. I hope when the legislation is brought forth that that party will not diddle-daddle and subvert the democratic and parliamentary process by refusing to debate legislation with innocuous points of order and disruptive tactics that do that party no good and the House of Commons no good either.

February 2, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
This is a black Friday, finishing off a black week for the CBC. On Tuesday Canadians were told about budget cuts totalling $140 million.
There were 400 or 500 jobs slashed. Today we get the news of a children's program chopped which is regionally produced in four centres and seen in most parts of the country. This is step by step dismantling of a great Canadian institution. The next thing we know the government will be telling Canadian kids that they cannot watch Mr. Dress-up.
Is it the government's objective to preside over the destruction of the CBC? Is that the goal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am told by members who attend the respective standing committee that the hon. member made quite a strong case about the fat that occurs in the CBC on Bronson Avenue. He made strong representations. Obviously, his representations have been taken into consideration by the management and they have acted.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister has just attacked the management of the CBC. He evades his own responsibility. It is quite clear what is happening. This government has slashed the CBC budget. The CBC has had no choice but to cut its regional program budget and this is not going to be the end of it. Down the road we are going to see program cuts at the network level. Canadians are not going to stand for this. What we are seeing is the slow death of the CBC, death by strangulation.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister this. When is the government going to take its responsibilities seriously and provide support and leadership and not just a knife to the CBC?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it abundantly clear to the hon. members of the House that I am not attacking the CBC management. As a matter of fact we are
supportive of the CBC management. We think they are doing a great job.
I would like to ask the hon. member whether he really meant what he said. Is he in favour of the cuts that have occurred on Bronson Avenue? Obviously the management has taken cognizance of his representations and they have acted on the basis of some recommendations that are coming from members of the committee. I think that is the way the parliamentary process should work and I congratulate him.

Mr. Speaker, the effects of the 7 per cent goods and services tax are a slap in the face to those Canadians who built this country.
My question to the Minister of Finance is this. How does this government plan to significantly compensate those seniors, including the 27,000 in my riding, living on fixed incomes, when we know the cost of day-to-day living will increase under this oppressive and regressive goods and services tax?

Mr. Speaker, I commented on this yesterday and I will comment again. There are a number of items that are not taxed under the goods and services tax which are of direct interest and concern to senior citizens: basic groceries, meals on wheels, meals served in nursing homes, charges for health and dental care, hospital and nursing-home care, prescription drugs, medical devices. No tax will be charged on residential rents, on municipal transit, passenger ferry service, legal aid services and other financial services.
Eighty-four per cent of seniors will receive the benefit of the goods and services tax credit which is a cheque that is paid in advance four times a year to people who are eligible to receive it. As I have said, 84 per cent will receive that credit. The result is that a large proportion of senior citizens will be better off after sales tax reform than before.
The hon. member is shaking her head. These are the conclusions that have been arrived at by people in the Department of Finance. They have certified these numbers and if my colleague, the hon. member, disagrees with those numbers she has the responsibility to state
February 2, 1990

precisely where those numbers are wrong. Otherwise she should not be leading senior citizens astray with this faulty information.

Mr. Speaker, many studies, including the Canadian Seniors Network report, disagree. They say seniors living on a tight budget near or below the poverty level will pay still more under this 7 per cent goods and services tax.
Clothing, services, home repairs.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might ask hon. members to allow the member to put her question.

Mr. Speaker, the clawback makes pensioners pay more. The 7 per cent goods and services tax will make pensioners pay more. When will this government accept its responsibility to seniors by providing them with security and an adequate standard of living and promise them that once the rate is set at 7 per cent, it will remain at 7 per cent; not 7 per cent this year, 9 per cent next year and 11 per cent by 1992?

Mr. Speaker, I hear again that the Liberal Party is supportive of continuing to pay seniors who are earning more than $50,000 for a program which we cannot afford. Surely the hon. member realizes the significance of the deficit and the debt problem that we are facing. Many seniors understand the significance of that. Many seniors have stated directly to me that they support our efforts to get the deficit down. That requires as broad a sharing of the burden as is possible.
For senior citizens, we have only asked those who are earning more than $50,000 to participate in sharing that burden. That amounts to 4.3 per cent of seniors to share partially and only 1.8 per cent of seniors will have to pay back, through the tax system, their full old age security payment. speechtext:
Last Wednesday, January 31, the hon. member for Okanagan-Simil-kameen-Merritt concluded his remarks in debate on second reading of Bill C-62, by moving that the House do now adjourn. That motion was subsequently defeated on a recorded division.
When debate was resumed on the bill, the hon. member for Edmonton East rose on a point of order to suggest that the House was still entitled to the opportunity to proceed to the 10 minute question and comment period on the hon. member's speech.

The hon. member for Churchill and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca have argued that the right to proceed with the 10-minute questions and comments period is the prerogative of the House, not that of the member who has just ended his remarks.
After listening to arguments the Chair deferred ruling on the point of order to check precedents and past practices and then recognized the hon. member for Calgary West.
The Chair indicated as well that the House would be allowed the 10-minute period if the point of order raised by the hon. member for Edmonton East were deemed to be legitimate.

The Chair is now prepared to offer a ruling. According to Standing Order 74(2), following the speeches of members speaking 20 minutes on the second reading of a
bill, a period of 10 minutes, if required, is provided for questions and comments. The rule does not mention any qualification which would prevent the House from claiming this 10 minutes.
By practice, however, it has been established that if proceedings are interrupted before the 10 minute period is reached or exhausted and the member is not present in the House when debate is resumed, the Chair will recognize the next member seeking the floor. It is also true that there have been occasions when members moved superseding motions that were negatived only to have the House cariy on to another member who was recognized without a claim being made for the 10 minute question and comment period.
On the other hand the House has frequently claimed its right to the 10 minute period after members have moved amendments to the motion for second reading or motions to extend the sitting in order to prolong the debate and the claim has not been denied.

However our research uncovered the fact that during second reading debate on a bill on March 14 and 15, 1985, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, now Member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, moved the adjournment of the House. The motion was defeated in the ensuing vote. When debate resumed the following day the hon. member asked for a 10-minute questions and comments period. Speaker Bosley ruled that the fact that the hon. member had concluded his remarks by moving a dilatory motion did not prevent the House from proceeding with the 10-minute period.
In the case now under consideration, which is practically a repeat performance of the precedent I have just referred to, the Chair must keep previous practice in mind and allow a 10-minute period when second reading debate on Bill C-62 resumes, if the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt is in the House to respond.

The Chair would like to thank all members for their understanding and for giving the Chair the necessary time to do some research and some reflection on this very technical point before rendering its decision.
