Madam Speaker, I commend the hon. member for putting to me a few questions on how the government intends to deal with multiculturalism. As I said in my speech, if he listened closely, we have $2.5 billion invested in multiculturalism and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation legislation.
He referred to cuts. While he put his question I wrote a word down: "Quality" rather than "quantity". Do we need so many people to do the work? Three people are doing the work of one. You certainly realized this, since you live in the Ottawa area, where an unbelievable number of people are working but are not giving their best performance, either at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or even in other departments. So we made cuts and I am convinced that the CBC's new president certainly will get from those who are left the same results as when there were three times the number of people needed.
The last question I did not understand altogether. I am sorry I was taking notes. But following the discussions we had this afternoon, following the way the government has been working for multiculturalism under the new act, I must say Canada is the only country in the world with a new act to treat everyone on an equal footing, whatever his or her colour, race or country of origin. We also have excellent immigration policies that do not exist in other countries, and certainly the hon. member is following closely what is going on globally. What we see in other countries is that refugees especially and even immigrants are not accepted unless they can bring four times what people are bringing to Canada. We are open, we accept immigrants, and we continue accepting them. All I am asking is that all Canadians treat those people

February 2, 1990
Supply
on an equal footing, that they treat them the same way as they themselves want to be treated.

Madam Speaker, it is indeed a sobering debate today. There is no value more fundamental to our society and our existence as human beings on this earth than our value for life, the potential and the worth of every human being. We often come closer to that in our rhetoric than in our practice, unfortunately. A member on the other side of the House said earlier this afternoon that it lies in our hands to lead by example.
I want to examine one particular aspect of equality in Canada. There is no more fundamental right of equality than the right to work, to earn a living and to earn a salary that reflects fully the value of the work one does. Yet in this field alone people of different cultural, ethnic and religious backgrounds are not treated equally in this country. They are not given the full opportunity to develop and demonstrate their potential and to be adequately compensated for it.
By allowing this to continue, we not only demean, belittle and diminish the lives of those people but we diminish the life of our nation. The most valuable resource we have is the capacity and the ability of our people to contribute to the future development of Canada and to the richness of Canadian life.
There is no better way for the Government of Canada to lead than to exercise the tremendous influence it has as the largest employer in Canada and to demonstrate that full equality in hiring, that eliminating biases and prejudices of which we may not even be aware, is so fundamental to acting as a good employer and, above all, to acting as a good government that it deserves the highest priority that this government and this House can give.
I have raised this issue a number of times in the House and have been subjected to rhetorical answers about our employment equity practices and employment equity program and what a wonderful job we are doing. The facts are quite otherwise. I think it is important for the House to be aware of those facts.
Indeed, the Public Service Commission has done a good job of encouraging people to apply for employment within the federal government. I want to talk about the category identified as visible minorities. The federal government between 1987 and 1988 encouraged a 250 per cent increase in applications by people of visible minorities. Of a total 56,000 applicants to public service fully 9,500 were from visible minorities. But how did they fare when it came to being hired? While the number of applicants increased by 250 per cent, the number hired increased by less than 100 per cent.
If your skin was a different colour than that of the Canadian majority, your chance of being hired was only one-quarter as good. Let me just give the figures. Of all applicants, 17 per cent were hired. Of visible minority applicants, only 3 per cent were hired. That means that there is a six to one discrimination factor in our hiring practices in government.
I turn to the report of the Human Rights Commission for 1988 where it states:
Although the official Treasury Board report published at the end of the year puts its best foot forward, analysis of the latest public service figures reveals that matters are not all that much better in federal departments and agencies, despite their having been subject to a policy on employment equity for several years.
It states further:
Visible minorities fair reasonably well in the professional group but their numbers are negligible in blue-collar categories and well below national workforce figures in other areas.
In fact in hiring people into management the federal government has a worse record than the private sector; 6.4 per cent of our workforce are identified as being visible minorities. Yet, in our management category, only 1.6 per cent are. We find visible minorities in the public service clustered in the professional categories, virtually excluded from blue-collar positions, and clustered again in the low-paying clerical worker jobs. On the other hand, the management category in the private sector is well over 2 per cent, more than double that of the federal government. This is nowhere near the ratio of visible minorities in the Canadian population or the Canadian workforce, but is double the record of the federal government.
The same situation applies to promotions. People do get into the Public Service of Canada but they stay where they are. They do not move up. They do not move into that management category where policies are being
February 2, 1990

made, where decisions are being made, where the very culturing ethos of the public service is being influenced and directed.
It is one of the reasons for my concern about Public Service 2000, the Canadian Centre for Management Development and various other initiatives of this government which would decentralize and delegate decision making. The Public Service Commission is responsible for hiring on the basis of the merit. But we have been unable to ensure that hiring is on this basis and not on extraneous factors such as the colour of the skin or the accent. I fear that by creating an elite management cadre we reinforce the little glass bubble lived in by our top 4,000 managers. We encourage and perpetuate the exclusion from that little glass bubble of those who do not quite fit.
There are pro-active ways to increase employment equity but they are not being carried out in the Public Service of Canada. There is no systematic sensitization of managers to the unconscious ways in which they may make choices of who to hire or who to promote. Essentially we all like to think of people who are most like ourselves as being competent. There is a desperate need for a pro-active program among managers in the public service to free up their thinking, to let them see and understand how they perhaps discriminate without intending to. There is also need for a pro-active program at the hiring level to work with people whose cultural differences, language barriers, and different backgrounds may be a negative factor in their being hired. We must get rid of those negative factors. There is a need to follow up when persons are not hired or interviewed to find out why and to what extent discrimination, however unconscious again, may have been a factor in that non-hiring.
There are a variety of areas in which Canadians look to the government for justice, fairness and equality. I was appalled earlier this year when this government refused to accept an amendment to the unemployment insurance bill that would have guaranteed equitable access for all discriminated groups to training and employment opportunities under the unemployment insurance scheme. I cannot understand or justify how our government, including the minister responsible for the Status of Women and the Secretary of State including people whose
Supply
responsibility is equality in Canadian society could have voted against that amendment. But they did.
I cannot understand why I get a letter from the Assembly of First Nations of Canada saying the Secretary of State has refused them literacy funding unless the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs approves. Are they not able to apply for a national program on the same basis as any other group of citizens in this country? Are they being told they do not qualify because they are native Canadians? These are the kinds of things that happen routinely in government that we must obliterate.
It is fine to speak nice words but we have to look at reality. We have to look at enumerators who go around during election time and see if they react differently to somebody with a different skin and ask them where they were bom. They do not ask that of people with white skin.
As the world opens up, people from different nations, different cultural and language backgrounds are invaluable assets to this country. They should be at the upper levels of policy-making, designing government programs, and they are not. I urge the members opposite to have an honest and open look at our own hiring and promotion practices and to fix them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the member who just spoke spent some time speaking about the public service and in reference to a very recent decision that was handed down concerning equal pay for work of equal value.
I would just like to read the decision on that particular issue brought forth by our government because we were concerned about the public service policy concerning the value of the jobs, and the pay. In January 1990, just last week, the President of the Treasury Board announced a $317 million retroactive equal pay adjustment covering four female dominated groups in the public service.
That retroactive adjustment will average about $4,800 per employee. Another $76 million will go to the annual adjustment taking effect in April of 1990. This is the result of work done since 1985 by the joint union management initiatives on implementation of the equal pay in the public service under which an employee study was undertaken and the value of 3,200 representative

February 2, 1990
Supply
jobs were assessed. Some 68 public servants will be affected by this adjustment.
That has been a veiy positive aspect of our government's initiative in terms of evaluating those jobs in the Public Service.
The other point I would like to bring to the attention of the member is the number of Order in Council appointments by this government of women who have been appointed to boards and commissions. When we took over in 1984, only 13 per cent of those positions were held by women; now it is 30 per cent. It should be 50 per cent, but women are being recommended for positions as they become available, as are visible minorities.
We recognize that there is more work to be done, but we have made giant strides in terms of what was needed.

Madam Speaker, the member can believe all the propaganda the minister wants to put out if she wishes to, but the Canadian Eluman Rights Commissioner has other things to say about that. He slams government over pay equity. He has attacked the government for not co-operating with the commission. He warns that the issue of pay equity in the federal public service is far from resolved. There are still 60,000 outstanding complaints before the Human Rights Commission. They have not been resolved. Forty-eight hundred dollars over five years is not pay equity. In fact, the latest settlement by the Human Rights Commission was four or five times that.
The member is obviously not aware that people do not get their salaries or classification increased when they win a pay equity settlement. They just get this little token payment on top. They are denied their benefits. They are denied benefits lost over the last five years or more.
I would ask the member to read the message from the Human Rights Commissioner who had offered his cooperation but was not consulted. He said that what Mr. de Cotret announced was, in fact, one-half of what these people deserve. However, all of this has nothing to do with equality in hiring practices. I urge you to look at the number of women, visible minorities, and persons with disabilities who are being hired on short-term, temporary contracts, and a part-time basis. They are not
getting into permanent jobs which would give them the financial security that people need and deserve.
I know people who have been in the public service for four or five years on repeating six months' terms, without any stability, security, promotion, or benefits.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am wondering how comfortable the member feels representing a party that had close to 20 consecutive years governing this country and left us with those pay equity problems? Is it comfortable to support a party that had 20 years to fix them but did nothing? Or is it more comfortable to support a party that has at least done something?
Five years and counting, Jim.

Madam Speaker, I think the member needs to be reminded that it is this party that introduced the Canadian Charter of Human Rights to ensure that not only in government, but throughout society, those problems would be addressed. It is his government which has had that charter for a number of years now and has been stalling and balking on implementing it.
I am not here to revisit history when attitudes were certainly different in government as they were throughout society. We know that the value of people and our commitment to respect the equality of people are something precious in our society. We incorporated equality in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in our Constitution.
Values are changing in society. Needs are changing in society. I think it is time the government took its responsibilities right now, stopped stalling and got on with the job.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The time for questions and comments is now over. On debate, the hon. member for Halifax.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak in strong support of this motion. I certainly advise the government Whip to listen; it might do him some good.
I rise to speak, as I said, in strong support of this motion and in a great deal of seriousness in relation to what has gone on today and what has gone on for far too long in this country: intolerance, bigotry and discrimination. These are synonyms for ignorance. They are syn-
February 2, 1990

onyms for fear. There is no place in the Canada of 1990 for words such as these nor for the sentiments that they portray.
Bigotry, prejudice and intolerance are not natural to the human species. They are learned responses, learned through odious example and passed on as an insidious legacy, eating away the fabric of decency in Canadian society. Anti-French, anti-woman, anti-black, anti-native, and so on: what we have is a perfidious, sickening litany of hate.
Unfortunately my riding of Halifax in my province of Nova Scotia now has a reputation that has been much tarnished over the past several years and, more unfortunately, rightly so. I refer to the report of the Marshall inquiry that has shown beyond any doubt the despicable treatment of visible minorities by the justice system and the institutionalized racism that exists in Nova Scotia.
However, the tragedy is that it exists not just in Nova Scotia. It exists in Canada as a whole. It exists in every province. Nova Scotians today bear the guilt for what has gone on in our province in the past, but as Canadians we jointly bear the responsibility for our refusal to come to terms provincially and federally with the questions of bigotry and intolerance.
The metropolitan area of Halifax and Dartmouth, as was referred to by my colleague, the member for Dartmouth, in his speech earlier today, contains the largest indigenous black population in Canada. Some 90 per cent of indigenous blacks live in Halifax and Dartmouth and the surrounding area. The black population of Nova Scotia has a long and proud history in this country.
Indeed black immigration to the east coast of Canada was in two ways. The first was a significant number of blacks who came as United Empire Loyalists after the American Revolution, who came with the idea of starting a new life loyal to the British Crown and who came under the same theories of land grants as their white counterparts. Unfortunately those theories were not realized. Although there are many blacks in Nova Scotia who can trace their roots to that same proud heritage, that proud heritage was never recognized in land grants and reactions from the British Crown. Perhaps this was the beginning of institutionalized racism in the province of Nova Scotia.
Supply
The second major wave of black immigration into Nova Scotia was the famous underground railroad from the southern states, run by such famed abolitionists as Harriett Beecher Stowe, her brother and various and sundry other brave and courageous anti-racists in the 19th century in the United States and Canada. The last stop on the underground railroad was the province of Nova Scotia. From there the communities such as Preston and Cherrybrook, the black communities in Cape Breton and Digby County and Yarmouth County, eventually arose.
Blacks in Nova Scotia have been nation builders, the same as Canadians of any other colour from coast to coast. In Nova Scotia blacks have laboured side by side with whites as coal miners and steel workers in some of the most back breaking and dangerous jobs this country has ever seen. They have been fishermen and they have been farmers. In my city of Halifax they are an integral part of the small but cosmopolitan community that is metropolitan Halifax.
Yet, despite all this contribution, we still have in the black community in my province a disproportionate unemployment rate and a disproportionate school leaving rate. Worst of all, we have a belief among the black community that its worth and its value to our society is less in the eyes of its white fellow citizens than it is in its own eyes. This a shame and a scandal and something that none of us can stand for while it still exists.
I want to talk very briefly about a particular part of my city: a particular housing project in the city of Halifax which I think is a microcosm of the problems created by racism, combined with poverty and combined with a refusal to see what is in front of us, a refusal to see the facts as they are.
Over 30 years ago this public housing project was built in the city of Halifax. It overlooks some of the most beautiful landscape in a beautiful city in a beautiful province. From this housing project one can see Bedford Basin, Halifax Harbour and the hills beyond Dartmouth. This project has a series of joined terraced houses and at least two or possibly three high-rise apartment buildings. The first thing that strikes one inside this complex is the amount of concrete and the absence of grass.

February 2, 1990
Supply
When I went there for the first time in many years this past summer, the first thing that struck me was: Who decided that people who live in public housing do not want to have grass for their children to play on just as much as people who live in expensive neighbourhoods? Who decided that concrete and rusty springs, broken cement and broken wrought iron are acceptable for the children of public housing residents when they are not acceptable for children of people in perhaps a higher economic bracket?
When we look at this particular housing project we see that discrimination is alive and well, because the vast majority of residents in this project are either black or another group vastly discriminated against in our society: single mothers probably on social assistance.
This project was built 30 years ago. In its high-rise elevators children are stopped and dealt drugs. Muggings and rampant crime against persons and against property are daily events. We all hear about the projects in Chicago and tell ourselves that our cities thus far are better off. Well, I am here to say that in my city of Halifax they are not better off. The project in Halifax may be smaller, but the harm to the humans, black and white, adults and children, who live there is no less.
I doubt that anyone in this House would ever admit to be racist. I doubt that anyone in this House would ever admit to being a bigot. Certainly I believe that all of us, no matter from where we come, no matter what views we espouse, are here because we want to do as much good as possible. When I say that I do not believe anyone in this House is truly a racist or a bigot, I hope it is true at least in the essential meaning of the word.
The problem is that while we sit here in this House of Commons and do no more about projects like Mulgrave Park, about a refusal to allow Sikhs to wear their turbans in the RCMP and about a refusal to grant pay equity as it is supposed to be granted, we plead guilty to the charges of intolerance.

Madam Speaker, I have a very brief comment to make and a question to direct to the member.
I congratulate her on the comments she made reflecting circumstances in her riding in Halifax which I visited many years ago and hope to visit some time in the future. I would also like to speak briefly to the motion presented by the Liberals on intolerance in our society in Canada.
It is a duty of all members of this House and community leaders to ensure that tolerance is recognized and continued in this country.
I gather this motion was presented by the Liberal Party. I am interested in having a comment from the member on how unified the Liberal Party is on the motion and if its members will be supporting it.
I refer to comments made on November 17 by the member for Gander-Grand Falls who in reference to the member's comments about turbans and Sikhs with the RCMP suggested that that was ridiculous. I wonder if Liberals have had their own talks on this issue so that they are in fact unified and that tolerance in society is represented by all members of all parties.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted with the question and comments of my colleague in the New Democratic Party. I can tell it has been a long time since he has been to Halifax, but I am sure he will remedy that. If he speaks to me, I will make sure they let him in.
With regard to a comment by my colleague for Gander-Grand Falls, if he said that the question of stopping the Sikhs from wearing their turbans in the RCMP was ridiculous, I can only say that I certainly agree. If he said something else, I suggest his remarks were misinterpreted. I am not familiar with the remarks. I only know that in the Liberal Party to which I belong I feel very strongly and I am fully aware that my views are supported by my caucus colleagues.
This is an issue that goes beyond partisan point making. If at times any one of us in any of the three parties falls from grace and makes a comment that is unacceptable to someone else, it is sad and unfortunate. We all try very hard to make sure that this does not happen, but unfortunately we too are human and we too make mistakes. When the day comes that we can stand here in this House and say that no one in any of the three parties is likely to put a foot wrong, perhaps that will be the day that this country will be in such perfect condition that we will have evolved ourselves out of the need for a job.

Madam Speaker, I was interested in what my colleague had to say about the obvious links between poverty and racism and lack of education and lack of opportunity. I just wonder if she might take a minute to reinforce her message to the House that
February 2, 1990

racism has some veiy undesirable social and economic impacts in our communities.

Madam Speaker, I have a very brief comment in response. I mentioned that there was a disproportionate school leaving rate for blacks and a disproportionate unemployment rate for blacks in the province of Nova Scotia. I would just like to quote some statistics very briefly. We have 10,000 people in the Nova Scotia Civil Service. The Marshall inquiry report has told us this week that only 208 of those civil servants are visible minorities, which includes not only blacks but other visible minorities as well.
Today the Premier of Nova Scotia, John Buchanan, said there was no racism in the Nova Scotia Civil Service, and he said that he could not recall any incident of discrimination within the Civil Service or even a charge thereto in the last 10 years.
I want to say that in a city like mine where blacks are continually and daily the subject of discrimination in education and in hiring a statement such as this one shows nothing short of irresponsibility and insensitivity of a mammoth nature.

Madam Speaker, intolerance and prejudice are attitudes that are crippling in any society, not only to individuals and families but also to society at large.
The House heard earlier today of government action on issues ranging from race relations and official languages to culture and justice, all of them fields in which this government's initiatives have made a meaningful difference in regard to improvements.
I join in the debate by discussing government initiatives in another field: the world of employment. I will focus on the issue of employment equity for there are few measures of such general significance in the fight against intolerance and prejudice.
This government recognized from the outset that Canada could no longer afford the enormous social and economic class implicit in inequitable and unjust employment barriers. We understood that for Canada to succeed in the 1990s and beyond the full participating of our human resources was essential.
Supply
Everyone in the House is aware that the competitive and skill demands on our labour market are increasing at an unprecedented rate. To meet these demands we must equitably involve all Canadians. In contrast to the government of hon. members across the floor, this government has not merely paid lip service to the issue of employment equity but we have acted decisively and responsibly.
In 1986 we took a number of major steps toward achieving equity in employment in Canada. As part of that initiative the government established two important programs: the legislative employment equity program and the federal contractors program. These major landmarks deal significantly and specifically with the four groups arbitrarily affected by stereotypes and prejudice, namely, women, aboriginal peoples, visible minorities and persons with disabilities.
The Employment Equity Act was passed in 1986. It is the first legislation of its kind. The legislative employment equity program applies to Crown corporations and to federally regulated employers with 100 or more employees. These employers are primarily in the banking, transportation and communications industries.
Under this program employers must implement employment equity and submit annual reports showing how the four designated groups are represented in their organization in terms of salary ranges, occupational groups, hiring, promotions and terminations. Their reports are analysed by us and are then made available to the public through public libraries. Employers who fail to report may be fined.
In addition, these reports are handed over to the Canadian Human Rights Commission which can take action against an employer who has discriminated.
It is important to note that this legislation does not set quotas or dictate exact steps employers must take. It is not a bureaucratic albatross for employers. Instead, it is a developmental mechanism which encourages investment in a more representative, productive workforce. The goal of these programs is to achieve equal access to employment opportunities for traditionally under-represented Canadians.
The government moved quickly to pass this legislation and we have been encouraged by the response from Canadian employers. The legislative employment equity program and the federal contractors program encompass

February 2, 1990
Supply
35 per cent of the top 500 companies in Canada with more than 1.5 million employees in total.
Under the the federal contractors program failure to implement an employment equity plan will result in sanctions, meaning that there will be no more opportunity to do business with the federal government until the program criteria have been met. This has already happened in many cases but, more important, over the short-term period we are seeing some positive results based on acceptance of this program and this government objective to put a more representative and dynamic face on our workforce.
We will continue to monitor these programs. We are determined to take the steps necessaiy to ensure even greater progress. Across Canada companies are recognizing that employment equity means good business. As important as this progress is the government sincerely believes that it is even more fundamental to give Canadians the chance to find their place in an expanding labour market. After all, the road to productive, meaningful employment must be built on economic opportunity.
Over the last five and a half years this government has clearly established a framework of opportunity and growth. During that time employment has fallen significantly, while job opportunities have grown. As significant as the number of jobs is the type of jobs this government is targeting. Through the Canadian Jobs Strategy approximately 1.5 million Canadians have received meaningful training and on the job experience since 1985. By emphasizing co-operative involvement with the private sector at the local level, the Canadian Jobs Strategy has given Canadians meaningful job skills that translate into long-term employment.
There has been no riding in the country that has benefited more from this particular program than the riding of Carleton-Charlotte. We have given programs to many disadvantaged people, especially women. We have allowed women to go into the workforce who have never had the opportunity because of lack of education, marital break-ups or whatever. We have really had some great successes in New Brunswick with that particular program. We have programs coming on stream constantly to address this very real need in the workforce.
Consistent with the Canadian Jobs Strategy mandate of helping those in need, participation in the CJS program is focused on women returning to the workforce, persons with disabilities, young people and other target groups.
This commitment to a more dynamic and representative workforce was reinforced last spring through the government's Labour Force Development Strategy. This strategy includes positive changes to the UI program designed to reflect the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as well as contemporary, social, family and work patterns. Again it is the co-operative, training oriented strategy involving all stakeholders in the common goal of making our labour force more responsive to emerging pressures.
Employment equity is not a thing of the past, but on a variety of legislative fronts this government has implemented measures that are already having an important impact. As the hon. member's motion states, every one of us in Parliament has a role to play in ensuring that all Canadians receive equitable hiring and salary treatment. This government has taken and is taking significant steps in that direction. The result of these initiatives and of a sustained period of economic growth has been unprecedented. The opportunity for Canadians will continue to grow.
In conclusion, the government is committed to ensuring that these opportunities continue to grow for all Canadians.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Resuming debate with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

Madam Speaker, I guess when one is almost the last one on the list in this debate one has an opportunity to do a bit of a recap.
On behalf of my party I thank the member for York Centre and the Liberal caucus for the presentation of this motion. Given some of the events in Canada today, it is important that we commit some time in this Parliament to the discussion of what appears to be a growing wave of racism and intolerance in this country.
It is of particular concern, when we look elsewhere in the world where barriers between peoples are breaking down, where freedom seems to be on the increase, where democratic thought seems to be on the increase and where tolerance to be on the increase, that in
February 2, 1990

Canada the tide may be moving the other way. This is something that we in this Parliament and that the government have to be concerned about.
Some members even mentioned the speech in Parliament a couple of days ago by Prime Minister de Klerk of South Africa in which he announced that the barriers in South Africa are to begin to be broken down and that an approach is to be made toward more equality between the races and the establishment of more equal rights between the races in South Africa.
As those countries which have in the past been less tolerant become more tolerant, my concern is that Canada seems to be proceeding in the opposite direction and at some point along the way will end up substituting for those countries as the object of international concern and derision.
Previous speakers have mentioned the motion recently made in Sault Ste. Marie about its establishment as a unilingual city. This country is proud of its bilingual traditions and wishes to see those traditions expanded and the rights of Canadians, regardless of their mother tongue, respected all across the country. What happened in Sault Ste. Marie recently came as a shock to many Canadians who see this country as a country of freedom, a country of tolerance and a country of mutual respect.
One thing that has disturbed me over the last little while is the number of letters and petitions I have been receiving from people in my constituency and elsewhere, suggesting that devout Sikh Canadians who wear the turban should not have the right to be members of the RCMP because it will interfere with the tradition of the RCMP uniform.
I have noticed in the letters these people have written that they always feel compelled to include in these form letters that: "This is not a prejudiced statement".
Of course it is a prejudiced statement. It is designed to limit access of a specific religious group to the national police force of Canada based on specific characteristics of their religious; either that or it forces them to divest themselves of important aspects of their religion in order to conform with what the balance of the Canadian society would like to see.
Supply
In spite of a recommendation from senior officers of the RCMP and in spite of the concerns expressed in this Parliament, it is unJfortunate that the Solicitor General has taken so long to make a decision on this issue.
Totally irresponsible.

It is not just irresponsible. It gives people out there in society, people who are members of minority groups, the message that this delay means there is an element of racism in the Government of Canada which gives rise to the delay in making a decision with respect to the opportunity for Sikhs to serve in the RCMP.
There is concern about racism in the government itself. I think that is a legitimate concern and something about which all of us in the this Parliament and this government have to be concerned.
The Minister of State for Multiculturalism said in his presentation that government alone cannot solve the problem of racism, that it has to be done with the co-operation of others. To some extent, that is true. I do not think government alone can solve the problem.
To some extent, this is a cop-out for taking strong and effective action to deal with racism when we perceive it operating in our society. I would like to go back a few years. Mention has been made about racism in the United States, especially racism directed against blacks.
In the 1940s and 1950s blacks were protected under the United States Constitution. They had equality before the law under the U.S. Constitution. In terms of education, blacks were supposed to have the same rights as every other American, and yet blacks did not have the same right to education.
All Americans were entitled to vote at that time and vote for their leaders and presidents. Yet blacks seemed to be deprived of that right to vote and to exercise power because of the way the system enforced the rights of black people in the United States. It was only when the segregation decision was taken by the courts and the United States federal government used the power of its military forces to put black kids into white schools that the changes took place in the United States with respect to equal access to education.

February 2, 1990
Supply
It was only when the federal government of the United States passed laws with respect to voter registration that they enforced the operation of those laws in favour of black citizens. By using armed Federal Bureau of Investigation agents, black people in the United States got the rights that were guaranteed to them under the Constitution and under the fundamental law of the United States.
There is a principle that operates here and that principle is before you can change attitudes, you must change behaviour. Before you change attitudes, you must change behaviour. Education cannot do it alone. Fine sentiments made and expressed in this House cannot do it alone. Before you change attitudes, you have to change behaviour.
Members brought up the issue of the employment equity legislation. I think this employment equity legislation is not anything that we can be proud of in this country. There is absolutely nothing that we can be proud of in terms of this legislation. The annual report of the Employment Equity Act documents the failure of this legislation to serve the very people that it purportedly was designed to serve.
In fact, Madam Speaker, this legislation is designed to be public relations. It is designed to be smoke and mirrors. When you look at the success of this legislation from the point of view of aboriginal people-and I will just take one page-of all the corporations listed under federal jurisdiction on page 81, only a miniscule number conform with the requirements for hiring aboriginal people.
Even the Canadian government's own Crown corporations and instruments, such as Canada Post Corporation, is a failure with respect to the hiring of aboriginal people. Yet it is under the direct control and responsibility of this Parliament and this government.
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has also been an absolute failure with respect to the hiring of women, aboriginal people, people with disabilities and members of visible minorities. Yet it is under the direct control and responsibility of this government and this Parliament.
There is no effective employment equity legislation in this country. The reason is that it was designed not to be effective because if people are designing legislation to accomplish employment equity, they must design that legislation to have within it the ability to impose sanctions against those who do not obey the law. Not to include such a section in this law is not an error or an omission; it is an invitation to the corporations that come under the federal jurisdiction to practice the biases that this law purports to be eliminating. That is precisely what is happening.
This is not a document designed to decrease prejudice or intolerance in this country. This document in fact increases it because it creates expectations without the ability of the people involved, the people oppressed, to have those expectations fulfilled. If this government does not within a very short period rectify this legislation so that it is designed to eliminate intolerance and prejudice, we are going to have something to say about this government and its commitment to eliminating racism and intolerance. These kinds of things do not happen in a country where the government has a commitment to eliminating intolerance. It is as simple as that.
Until we see some changes in this legislation, we are not going to see changes in the performance of those corporations. Then we are going to have some questions to ask about this government's commitment to eliminating racism and intolerance.
Some members in this debate mentioned the Marshall inquiry that recently reported in Nova Scotia. I think we should all read the report of that Marshall inquiry. It says a great deal about Canada. It says a great deal about Canadians and about the institutions of Canada and how they are racially biased against non-whites in Canada.
I would like to quote a few short sections of the Marshall inquiry. Basically, what the Marshall inquiry says in the very first part of its findings in fact its most important findings, is this: "The fact that Marshall was a native was a factor in his wrongful conviction and imprisonment."
It is the most unbelievable finding in this report. The most important finding in the Marshall inquiry report is the fact that Marshall was a native was a factor in his wrongful conviction and imprisonment.
There is a second section: "That MacIntyre without any evidence to support his conclusions and in the face of evidence to the contrary, had identified Marshall as a prime suspect. The fact that Marshall was a native was
February 2, 1990

one of the reasons why MacIntyre identified him as the prime suspect."
The judicial system in Canada discriminates against people in Canada because they are of a different colour or a different culture than those of the dominant culture. That is the true finding of the Marshall inquiry.
We really did not need the Marshall inquiry to find this out. All you have to do is read the statistics of native people in prisons in Canada to find out exactly how this country's justice system discriminates against native people.
Let me quote from an article entitled "Locking up Natives in Canada" by Michael Jackson, a professor at the University of British Columbia. He talks about the federal prison system, the system this Parliament and this government has direct responsibility for. Here is what Michael Jackson says: "Ten per cent of the federal prison population is native men; 13 per cent in the women's prison are native women, and yet native people are only 2 per cent of the population."
You cannot argue from the point of view that natives are more criminally oriented, more likely to be involved in crime and more likely to be involved with brushes with the law. The system of justice in Canada is culturally and racially biased against native people and statistics document this over and over again. You do not need the Marshall report. You do not need the justice enquiry that is going on in Manitoba. You do not need the justice inquiry that is going on in Alberta. The statistics document over and over again that Canada is a de facto racist society when it comes to the practice of administering injustice against native people. This Parliament and this government have an obligation to do something about that.
In the prairie region natives make up 5 per cent of the total population but 32 per cent of the prison population. We send natives to jail at a rate six times greater than their representation in the population. It is de facto evidence that our system of justice and our country are discriminating on a racial basis against native people. This is not a finding that comes out of things like the Marshall inquiry alone. This is a finding that is now
Supply
coming out of human rights agencies set up by the United Nations.
People are beginning to recognize throughout the world that this Canada of ours, this country that we expressed such great pride in at the opening of this debate, this country of ours has nothing to brag about when it comes to racial equality or equal treatment before the law. It is not only in the justice system where we discriminate against natives.
There is an editorial I would like to refer to called "Our Third World" in the Edmonton Journal of January 21, 1990:
Alberta's treaty Indians suffer tuberculosis at a rate 12 times higher than the provincial average. Add in Metis and non-status Indians and the TB rate in the native community doubles. These 1988 stats follow a long trend of TB rates that run 10 to 20 times higher among natives than among non-natives.
Tuberculosis is essentially a disease of poor people who live in miserable conditions of housing and nutrition and natives suffer from this disease 10 to 20 times more than the general population.
Natives suffer a higher incidence of skin disease, diabetes, high blood pressure. The death rate from respiratory diseases is two times the Canadian rate. From injury and poisoning four times the Canadian rate. From suicide three times the Canadian rate.
In fact, Indians die at a rate two to four times higher than non-natives in this country at every age up to 54. Their life expectancy is nine years shorter than non-native Canadians, shorter even than the life expectancy in some Central American countries.
This country has an institutionalized system of discrimination on the basis of race against native Indians. We cannot make eloquent statements here about how good Canada is or how good we are going to be unless we come up with some concrete measures in this Parliament to deal with the issue and do something about it. To do something about it, Madam Speaker, you must change behaviour before you change attitudes. You have to change the law, you have to provide sanctions in the law and you have to be tough in the enforcement of that law.
We want to live together in this country with all people of all walks of life of all creeds and colours. But to do it we have to afford the same protection to all that we afford to ourselves. I think out of this debate Parliament should make a strong commitment that it intends to do that very thing.

February 2, 1990
